Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Heathrow airport Heathrow passengers face disruption after flood restricts access Airport advises passengers travelling from terminals 2 and 3 to use rail and tube as pipe leak closes road Daniel Lavelle Sat 15 Aug 2026 06.36 EDT Last modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Heathrow airport has warned of disruption after flooding caused by a pipe leak restricted access to terminals 2 and 3. Water in the central terminal area means anyone trying to travel to or from either terminal is unable enter by road. Passengers are being advised to travel by rail and tube instead. Access to the terminal car parks is also impeded, leaving passengers with parked cars unable to access them. An airport spokesperson said: “Our teams are working to resolve the situation as quickly as possible. We apologise for any disruption caused. The leak has been isolated and repairs are ongoing.” The disruption comes during the school holidays, one of the airport’s busiest periods. Heathrow said 19 July had been its busiest day of the year so far with more than 267,000 passengers passing through as many schools broke up for summer. The airport was recently affected by disruption to rail services after a water leak prompted the closure of a tunnel. The airport is one of the busiest in the world, with as many as 1,300 flight movements – takeoffs and landings – every day. Heathrow announced the latest disruption on X, leading to a stream of queries and complaints from concerned travellers. “Do we have to meet and greet at T4 or 5?? When will this be resolved?,” one asked. An official response read: “We recommend heading to T5 M&G and explaining to staff that your booking has been affected by the flooding.” Another said: “I am collecting my daughter from Terminal 3 shortly; she has special needs. She has travelled via a wheelchair. Please can you advise?” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The airport replied: “You would not be able to park at Terminal 3 currently as there is no access by road; you would need to park at Terminal 4 or 5 and transfer to Terminal 3. We do have assistance teams in the terminal who would be able to advise on the best way of returning to your vehicle with a wheelchair passenger.” The consumer rights group Which? urged passengers to check airline policies on booked flights, and advised against unnecessary travel. The editor of Which? Travel, Rory Boland, said: “Passengers heading to Heathrow today will understandably be worried, so it’s important to follow the airport’s advice and avoid travelling by road to Terminals 2 and 3, instead allowing extra time and using public transport where possible. “If you’re worried you may miss your flight because of the disruption, contact your airline as soon as possible. Airlines have different policies on missed flights, so it’s worth finding out if you are entitled to a free rebooking or refund if your flight has operated. “If you’ve paid for airport parking but can no longer use it because of the road closures, contact the parking provider as soon as possible to see if you can amend your booking or get a refund. You should also check your travel insurance to see whether you’re covered for any costs you incur because of the disruption, such as a missed flight or additional travel expenses.” Explore more on these topics Heathrow airport Air transport Transport Flooding news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Heathrow says need for expansion clear as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airport Heathrow expects fall in passengers and profits this year because of Iran war Heathrow third runway GDP yield may be 90% less than previous estimates Heathrow third runway likely to harm health of millions nearby, official report warns Heathrow could be forced to allow other firms to build third runway to cut costs Heathrow passenger numbers dip as demand for international travel ebbs amid Iran war fallout Heathrow in talks with airlines to end row that could delay third runway UK aviation regulator rejects Heathrow’s plans to significantly raise landing fees Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

http://www.bgnes.com/politics/hungary-at.text: BGNES Politics Hungary at a Crossroads: Institutional Cleansing and the Dawn of a Post-Orbán Era Hungary at a Crossroads: Institutional Cleansing and the Dawn of a Post-Orbán Era 13.08.2026 - 19:32 Share BGNES The cornerstone of this political shift is the recent election of 73-old legal scholar András Baka as the new President of Hungary. Hungary is currently undergoing a profound systemic transformation as the country navigates a new political reality following the end of Viktor Orbán’s 16-year nationalist rule. Prime Minister Péter Magyar and his pro-EU conservative Tisza party, which now holds a two-thirds majority in parliament, have embarked on a comprehensive mission to dismantle the lingering influence of what has been described as a "captured state." This ambitious agenda of restoring the democratic rule of law is manifesting simultaneously through sweeping political changes at the highest levels of government and stringent new economic regulations aimed at mending the country’s fractured relationship with the European Union. The cornerstone of this political shift is the recent election of 73-year-old legal scholar András Baka as the new President of Hungary. The position became vacant after the controversial removal of the previous president and Orbán ally, Tamás Sulyok. Sulyok’s mandate was abruptly terminated through a constitutional amendment-a move that, while effective for the new government, drew criticism from rights watchdogs who compared the legislative tinkering to the illiberal methods previously employed by Orbán. Consequently, Orbán’s Fidesz party and its ally KDNP boycotted the parliamentary vote, denouncing the ouster as tyrannical and illegitimate. In their absence, Baka was elected in a secret ballot with 140 votes from the Tisza parliamentary group, while the six MPs from the far-right Mi Hazánk party presumably voted against him. Baka’s ascension to the presidency is heavily symbolic of Hungary's return to constitutional governance. A highly respected jurist who obtained his doctorate from ELTE in 1978, Baka served as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) for 17 years. In 2009, he was appointed head of the Supreme Court, but his tenure was cut short in 2011 by the Fidesz government, which abruptly lowered the mandatory retirement age for judges from 70 to 62 in retaliation for his repeated criticisms of their judicial reforms. Baka successfully challenged his dismissal, with the EU’s top court and the ECHR ruling in 2012 and 2016 that his premature removal violated both EU law and his freedom of expression. His election today serves as a powerful vindication and a guarantee that the restoration of liberal democracy is on track. Baka is expected to serve a transitional term of no more than five years, or until a new constitution-drafted through a broad public consultation process slated to begin next month and lasting up to 18 months-is officially adopted. However, the path to finding the right head of state was not without political missteps. As reported by EUobserver, Prime Minister Magyar initially faced internal backlash after hastily offering the presidency to world-renowned chess legend Judit Polgár, breaking a promise to hold public consultations. Polgár declined the role amid outrage from within the Tisza camp, where many argued that a lawyer was needed for the position and criticized the lack of debate. Following an apology from Magyar, the selection process became far more measured. The leadership held meetings with prominent figures such as historian Ignác Romsics and lawyer Botond Fülöp-the man instrumental in exposing the pedophile-pardon scandal that previously brought down former President Katalin Novák and Justice Minister Judit Varga. Ultimately, selecting Baka was a calculated strategic move. While analysts like Dániel Róna, director of the 21 Kutatóközpont research centre, noted in the EUobserver coverage that parliamentary speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer might have been a more popular choice, Baka provides a principled, independent counterweight who will not automatically sign every piece of government legislation, yet remains unlikely to become a political or social media rival to Prime Minister Magyar. Parallel to this constitutional reset, Budapest is executing critical economic reforms to unlock frozen EU funds. The Hungarian Integrity Authority has launched a publicly accessible register to blacklist economic operators from public procurement if their key figures-such as executive officers, supervisory board members, managing directors, or beneficial owners-have final court convictions for criminal offenses defined in the Public Procurement Act. While the primary goal is to prevent further abuse of public funds rather than mere stigmatization, the government has also introduced an electronic, ex officio "self-cleaning" procedure. Companies can petition to be removed from this blacklist if they can thoroughly document that they have compensated the injured parties for the damages caused, actively cooperated with competent authorities to clarify the facts, and implemented robust technical, organizational, and personnel measures to prevent future offenses. The relevant authorities are mandated to assess these appeals within 20 days, continuously updating the Electronic Public Procurement System. Ultimately, these combined efforts illustrate a nation aggressively pivoting away from an era of entrenched political loyalty and systemic corruption. By installing a president with a proven track record of defending judicial independence and simultaneously implementing strict, transparent economic safeguards, Hungary’s new leadership is laying the groundwork for a transparent, European-aligned future, even as it navigates the delicate internal politics of transitioning away from an illiberal past. | BGNES Follow us also on Watch and Comment news More from Politics US Lawmakers Step Up Pressure on Vučić, Propose Sanctions Over Democratic Backsliding 27.08.2026 - http://www.thetibetpost.com/outlook/op-e.text: Details Yeshe Choesang 15 July 2026 Tibet was always known to be a country until China invaded and took it over. The National Flag of Tibet at a military parade in Lhasa, Capital of Tibet in 1938. Photo: File Op-Ed Hub Previous Article The architecture of complicity: how the UN’s silence empowered totalitarian erasure in Tibet Next Article Xi Wages a War on Truth, Freedom, and Historical Memory to Revive Maoist Totalitarianism Typography Smaller Small Medium Big Bigger Default Helvetica Segoe Georgia Times Reading Mode Share This The statement issued by the Chinese Embassy in Estonia is not an objective response to the legitimate concerns raised by a democratic parliament; rather, it represents a familiar pattern of political deflection, historical revisionism, diplomatic intimidation and the selective management of historical memory concerning Tibet. Topic The great betrayal of Tibet Tibetans Protest with Photos of 171 Self-Immolators, Condemn UN Failure to deliver justice for Tibet Tibetans begin “Peace Walk for a Free Tibet” to carry on Lobga Rangzen’s final call The architecture of complicity: how the UN’s silence empowered totalitarian erasure in Tibet Lobga Rangzen Biography: Tibetan Activist Advocating for the Independence of Tibet Lobga Rangzen's Final Statement: All the root causes of our problems stem from the loss of Tibet's Independence The Embassy's attempt to dismiss the landmark statement signed by a majority of Members of the Estonian Parliament cannot obscure a fundamental reality: fifty-one elected representatives of a sovereign democratic nation exercised their legitimate right to express concern regarding China's policies in Tibet. Instead of engaging with the substance of the parliamentary statement, the Embassy repeated familiar accusations of "interference in China's internal affairs", support for "Tibetan independence", spreading "lies" and violating China's sovereignty. Such accusations have become a standard response whenever governments, legislators, journalists, academics or international organisations raise concerns about China's human rights record. Political slogans, however, do not constitute evidence, and repeated claims of sovereignty cannot replace transparent examination of historical facts, human rights concerns and international obligations. The Embassy's assertion that China fully protects ethnic minority rights stands in direct contradiction to extensive documentation produced over decades by United Nations human rights experts, independent researchers, international organisations and scholars concerning restrictions on Tibetan language education, religious freedom, cultural expression, movement, peaceful assembly and freedom of expression. If China's policies in Tibet genuinely enjoy the international recognition claimed by Beijing, there would be no need for such extensive restrictions on independent journalists, international observers, United Nations mechanisms and foreign researchers seeking access to Tibetan areas. Instead, Tibet has become one of the most tightly controlled regions in the world, where information is heavily regulated, surveillance is widespread and peaceful expressions of Tibetan identity are frequently portrayed as political threats. The Embassy's assertion that Tibet has always been an inseparable part of China represents the official position of the People's Republic of China, but it remains a contested historical and political claim rather than an uncontested fact. Tibet maintained its own governmental institutions, legal system, currency, taxation system, postal services, diplomatic relations and armed forces before the People's Liberation Army entered Tibet in 1950. Similarly, Beijing's increasing replacement of the internationally recognised name "Tibet" with "Xizang" cannot be understood merely as a linguistic preference. For many Tibetans and international observers, this terminology campaign represents an attempt to redefine historical identity, narrow the geographical meaning of Tibet, reshape global discourse and gradually erase the historical consciousness of the Tibetan people. The most fundamental issue raised by the Estonian Parliament's statement is therefore not a matter of political disagreement but a question of historical responsibility, moral credibility and universal human rights principles. China's so-called Law on Ethnic Unity and Progress, criticised by the Riigikogu, is viewed by many Tibetans and observers as an instrument of assimilation rather than genuine cultural protection, through policies involving expanded Mandarin-language education, ideological control, increased surveillance, demographic restructuring and restrictions on expressions of Tibetan identity. A government that claims to understand the trauma of national humiliation should be the last to impose comparable forms of domination upon another people. If the Chinese Communist Party genuinely believes that invasion, occupation, repression, coercion and the loss of dignity experienced by the Chinese people during the so-called "Century of Humiliation" constitute profound historical injustices, then it carries an even greater moral responsibility not to reproduce similar experiences against Tibetans. Historical suffering should create empathy and a commitment to prevent injustice, not become a justification for imposing comparable forms of control over another nation or people. If the principles invoked through China's historical narrative are universal, they must apply equally to Tibet. A government cannot demand recognition of its own historical wounds while denying the identity, dignity and historical experiences of another people. The response of Estonia's Parliament therefore represents not hostility towards China or the Chinese people, but a defence of universal principles: that sovereignty cannot be used as a shield against accountability, that cultural diversity cannot be preserved through forced assimilation, and that no government should expect the world to remain silent while fundamental rights and historical identities are being diminished. The official campaign to replace the internationally recognised name "Tibet" with "Xizang" sends a powerful message to the world that China is intensifying a decades-long effort to reshape historical memory, redefine Tibet's identity and institutionalise policies that many Tibetans regard as oppressive, humiliating and assimilatory. This is not merely a matter of administrative terminology or linguistic preference; it represents, from the perspective of many Tibetans, a broader political strategy to control historical narratives, weaken international recognition of Tibet's distinct identity, and subordinate Tibetan language, religion, culture and collective memory to a state-defined national framework. By seeking to transform the internationally recognised identity of Tibet into a political designation created and controlled by the Chinese state, Beijing is attempting not only to alter a name but also to control how history is remembered, interpreted and transmitted to future generations. For Tibetans, these measures are viewed as a continuation of more than seven decades of political domination, cultural assimilation and restrictions on fundamental rights following China's military entry into Tibet in 1950. The effort to replace the name "Tibet" with "Xizang" is therefore perceived not as a neutral administrative decision, but as part of a broader attempt to diminish Tibet's historical consciousness, weaken its civilisational identity and transform the Tibetan people into conformity with a state-controlled vision of national unity. The issue extends far beyond terminology; it concerns the survival of a people's historical memory, cultural continuity and right to maintain a distinct identity. This development exposes a profound contradiction at the centre of China's historical memory narrative: the repeated invocation of its own "Century of Humiliation" while rejecting international scrutiny of policies that many Tibetans experience as domination, assimilation and identity erasure. A government that claims to understand the trauma of national humiliation should be the last to impose comparable forms of domination upon another people. If the Chinese Communist Party genuinely believes that the suffering, invasion, occupation, repression, coercion and loss of dignity experienced by the Chinese people during that historical period constitute profound injustices, then it carries an even greater moral responsibility not to inflict similar experiences upon others. Historical suffering should create empathy, humility and a commitment to prevent injustice—not become a political instrument for justifying comparable forms of control, assimilation and identity erasure against another people. Yet, from the perspective of many Tibetans, China's policies in Tibet since the 1950 invasion have produced precisely the forms of political domination, cultural suppression, historical revisionism and identity erosion that Beijing condemns when recounting its own historical grievances. The suppression of Tibetan language, restrictions on religious institutions, political control over cultural expression, rewriting of Tibetan history and attempts to replace Tibet's internationally recognised identity are viewed by many Tibetans as evidence that China has failed to apply to others the very principles it demands the world recognise for itself. This contradiction fundamentally undermines the credibility of the Chinese Communist Party's repeated invocation of the "Century of Humiliation." If the principles embodied in that narrative are genuine and universal, they must apply equally to Tibet. A government cannot demand permanent recognition of its own historical wounds while denying the historical experiences, identity and dignity of another people. If historical suffering is remembered as a moral lesson only when China was the victim, but rejected when Tibetans raise their own grievances, then the narrative risks appearing not as a universal condemnation of oppression, but as a selective political instrument used to strengthen national legitimacy while dismissing the suffering of others. The fundamental question is therefore one of moral consistency and historical responsibility: if China condemns invasion, occupation and humiliation when describing its own past, how can it justify policies that many Tibetans experience as producing similar consequences? If the lessons of history are genuine, they must be applied universally. A people who demand recognition of their own historical suffering cannot reasonably deny another people's right to preserve their language, culture, identity and collective memory. Ultimately, a government does not gain moral authority merely by possessing economic power, military strength or international influence; it earns credibility through consistency between the principles it claims to uphold and the actions it takes towards others. A nation that truly understands the consequences of humiliation should never become the source of similar experiences for another people. The landmark statement endorsed by a majority of Members of the Parliament of Estonia (Riigikogu) represents a historically significant and principled contribution to the international discussion on Tibet, challenging attempts to monopolise historical narratives and reaffirming that unresolved historical questions cannot be permanently silenced through political power alone. By explicitly recognising Tibet as "a country historically independent and forcefully occupied by the People's Republic of China (PRC)," the Estonian Parliament has moved beyond cautious diplomatic language and acknowledged that the Tibet issue cannot be understood solely through Beijing's contemporary political narrative, but must also be examined through its historical and political context prior to the People's Liberation Army's military entry into Tibet in 1950. The Riigikogu's statement further identifies China's Law on Ethnic Unity and Progress as a serious threat to Tibetan identity, warning that policies involving mandatory Mandarin-language education, expanded surveillance, ideological control, demographic restructuring and restrictions on cultural expression risk accelerating the erosion of Tibet's language, religion, historical consciousness and distinct identity. By declaring that such legislation has "no moral legitimacy in the eyes of the Tibetan people," the Estonian Parliament has affirmed that state authority alone cannot provide legitimacy to laws that undermine the fundamental rights and identity of a people. Its call for greater international engagement, United Nations attention, diplomatic pressure and a peaceful resolution of the China–Tibet conflict through genuine dialogue reflects not hostility towards China, but a commitment to the principles of accountability, cultural protection and human dignity. Estonia's own historical experience of occupation, the restoration of sovereignty and the preservation of national identity provides a powerful context for its solidarity with Tibet, demonstrating that smaller nations can play a meaningful role in defending historical memory, international law and the rights of peoples facing domination by more powerful states. The recent recognition of Tibet's historical status by the Parliament of Estonia is not the first instance of international advocacy concerning Tibet. El Salvador holds a unique and historically significant place in the international discussion on Tibet as the first country to advocate for Tibet's sovereignty at the United Nations, submitting a draft resolution titled "Invasion of Tibet by Foreign Forces" in 1950. By bringing the situation of Tibet before the United Nations, El Salvador demonstrated that Tibet's political status and the question of foreign military intervention were matters deserving international attention. The resolution represented an early expression of concern regarding the principles of sovereignty, the consequences of invasion and the rights of peoples affected by the actions of more powerful states. El Salvador's initiative remains historically significant because it established one of the earliest examples of Tibet's sovereignty being raised within a global diplomatic forum. More than seven decades later, this action continues to reflect the importance of international advocacy, demonstrating that the voices of smaller nations can contribute to discussions on justice, sovereignty, human dignity and the protection of peoples facing political challenges beyond their borders. The international raising of Tibet's political status continued beyond El Salvador's 1950 initiative. In 1965, Nicaragua and the Philippines joined El Salvador in submitting a joint letter to the United Nations Secretary-General to raise the "Question of Tibet." This action represented a continued effort by member states to bring attention to Tibet within the framework of international diplomacy and demonstrated that concerns regarding Tibet remained part of discussions at the United Nations. By formally presenting the issue through a joint communication, Nicaragua, the Philippines and El Salvador contributed to the continued international consideration of Tibet's political situation, reflecting the willingness of smaller nations to use diplomatic channels to raise questions relating to sovereignty, justice and the rights of peoples. Over more than seven decades of Tibet's freedom struggle, including the more than 170 known self-immolations by Tibetans inside and outside Tibet, individuals have made the ultimate personal sacrifice to draw international attention to their appeals for dignity, freedom, cultural survival and the right of the Tibetan people to preserve their identity and homeland. These acts represent a profound expression of despair regarding decades of political repress

https://www.politico.eu/article/us-fight.text: An F-16 Fighting Falcon fighter jet assigned to the U.S. Air Force’s 52nd Fighter Wing crashed at Spangdahlem Air Base in western Germany on Tuesday afternoon. The aircraft came down at around 2:30 p.m. local time, the 52nd Fighter Wing told POLITICO. The pilot ejected safely and received immediate medical care from emergency-response personnel. An investigation into the incident is ongoing, and “additional information will be released as it becomes available,” the spokesperson said. German air traffic control told German outlet SWR that the crash followed an exercise involving several aircraft . Other planes diverted to Ramstein air base after the incident. Advertisement Advertisement Emergency crews from the Eifelkreis Bitburg-Prüm district’s fire and disaster-protection services also responded. “One person was injured,” the district said in a statement , adding that “the emergency response measures have since ended.” It said could not provide further details about the circumstances of the crash. The 52nd Fighter Wing operates F-16 fighter jets in support of U.S. and NATO missions. In October 2019, a U.S. F-16 crashed near Zemmer-Rodt, south of the base, during a routine training flight. The pilot ejected and suffered minor injuries. A spokesperson for the German Defense Ministry wouldn't confirm or deny that the incident happened. This article has been updated.
